title: The temple of his body (John 2:13–25)
hook: destroy this temple and in three days I'll raise it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana, and the good wine kept until now. Your line was the best was kept till last. What good thing did you save and give away? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

If you read Luke with us, you already know this scene. Jesus in the temple, driving out the traders. But in Luke it comes at the end, in the last week. John puts it here, in chapter two, right at the start. Christians explain that in different ways. Some think it happened twice, once early and once late. Many scholars think John placed it at the start on purpose, so it would frame the whole story. Either way, it's Passover, the city is full, and Jesus walks into the outer court of the temple and finds it full of cattle, sheep, doves, and the tables of money changers.
screen: `LUKE PUTS IT LAST; JOHN PUTS IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Those traders were serving a real need. Pilgrims arriving from far away needed animals for the offerings, and coins the temple would accept. But Jesus makes a whip of small cords, drives out the sheep and oxen, pours out the coins, and turns over the tables. To the dove sellers he says: "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." My Father's house. The leaders ask him for a sign: what gives you the right? And he answers with a riddle: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." They hear it literally, and who wouldn't? "Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" Herod's great rebuilding project had been going on for decades. Then John tells us what the listeners missed: "But he spake of the temple of his body." The temple was where heaven and earth met, the place where God's presence lived among the people. Jesus is saying that place is now a person. His own body is where God dwells. Here's the honest part: John says even the disciples didn't get it at the time. Only after he was raised from the dead did they remember he'd said this, and believe. Christians later carried the idea one step further. Paul reminds the church in Corinth that "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you." So the body, the ordinary body that gets tired and hungry and sore, is treated as holy ground.
screen: then, large: `BUT HE SPAKE OF THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your body as a temple. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and slowly move your attention up: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face. Notice where you're tired, or tense, or sore. Don't judge it. Just notice. Then choose one kind thing you'll do for your body today. A glass of water. A walk. An early night. Stretching the place that hurts. Not to fix how you look, but to honor where you live. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body. The bell holds the time.
The temple of his body. What Jesus meant by destroy this temple: his own body, where God dwells, raised on the third day.
screen: `THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a temple of flesh. Today, do one kind thing for your body, a glass of water, a walk, an early night, as if it were holy ground. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christians read John's account of the temple in Lent in many churches, and Paul's words that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit shape Christian teaching about health, rest and the care of the body.

fork.reveal: "destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." they hear a building. John says he spoke of the temple of his body.

original.note: Greek: the sanctuary, the inner house of God. John uses it for 'this temple' in 2:19, not the word for the whole temple complex.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus lost his temper at the temple traders.
what it means: a sign that the meeting place of God and people is now a person, his body, destroyed and raised in three days.
what a scholar hears: John uses hieron for the temple courts and naos, sanctuary, for 'this temple'; and he places the scene at the start, unlike the Synoptics.

notes: One cleansing or two: presented as 'some think twice; many scholars think John placed it early'. Confirm fairness.
Traders and money changers serving pilgrims (offerings, Tyrian shekels for the temple tax): common background. Confirm. The script avoids framing the temple or Judaism as corrupt.
